$comment: Per-mission atmosphere for the remaster's volumetric fog.
Anything omitted falls back to 'default', and a mission with no entry at all is derived from its
own FlatSky task -- so this file only has to hold the levels where the derived value is wrong.
Density is extinction per metre at baseHeight; heightFalloff is the metres over which it thins to
a third, and is what makes fog pool rather than hang as a sheet. uniformFraction is the share of
it that does NOT thin with height -- raise it on a level whose playable ground is well above the
median, or the player standing on a ridge climbs clean out of the atmosphere.
baseHeight is NOT authored here: it is the level's own sky-plane height, anchored at load to the
scene's ground. Volume centres, however, ARE authored, and they are ABSOLUTE world metres -- a
level's coordinates sit tens of kilometres from the world origin, so a hand-guessed centre near
zero lands nowhere near the level. Read real ones off with -freecam plus -camlog, which prints the
camera position every frame: fly to the middle of the room and copy it down. Retail has no fog
entities of any kind, so every volume here is the port's own invention.
dust and dustIndoor are the fine dust any air holds, per metre: it scatters the sun and the lamps
and nothing else, so it is what a shaft of light through a window or a floodlight's cone at night is
seen in. dust thins out over the first forty-five metres from the eye; dustIndoor fills rooms, where
the medium itself is nought.
A bare key is Project I.G.I.'s mission; the sequel's are keyed igi2:<n>, where n is the mission's own id:
its location and its level read together, so location1/level1 is igi2:11 and location2/LEVEL6 is igi2:26.
Density stays the remaster's own, derived from the FlatSky fade where a mission sets none. It is far
thicker than the original's GlobalLight air on purpose: the second mission's valley mist is the look
players know the remaster by, and the original's own band is a thirtieth of it.
paintedSky keeps that share of the level's own painted dome and cloud layers over the atmosphere at
the hour the level was painted for (fading out over the three hours either side). exposureStops
moves a mission's brightness. nightBake lays that share of the shipped lightmaps under the moon at
full night -- a hundredth lands a night mission's ground on vanilla's own brightness; a tenth turns
the night back into day.
A night that reads too bright or too dark is tuned with the night-only fields, which leave the day
alone. moonlight, nightSky and nightAdaptation are multiples of the player's r_moonlight, r_night_sky
and r_night_adaptation (0.5 halves the setting), so every preset keeps its say. nightExposureStops
moves the brightness in stops at full night, faded in with the night. nightFog is how much of the
moon and the night sky the mission's fog catches at full night against its day (0.5 halves it): a
thin haze under a bright moon glows across the whole sky, and this dims that glow alone. nightHalo
scales the fog's forward scatter (its anisotropy) at full night: the lobe that gives a low sun its
glow gathers the moon into a halo far wider than a real moon wears; 0.5 keeps a soft one. nightGlow
multiplies the night sky's own glow (r_night_airglow): the light a night has without its moon, which
is what a valley keeps when the moon drops behind a ridge.

1.$comment: Cold clear morning over snow. THIN -- earlier passes read as overcast, nothing like the retail's crisp clear morning. The wash that hung even on near buildings was the flat terms, not distance: a 0.12 uniform fraction laid fog at every height and a 0.35 multiple-scattering glow lit it like a light-box. Cut both right down and drop the density to 0.0008, so what is left is a thin aerial depth on the far mountains and clear air over the yard. Forward scatter eased too, since a low sun through the denser lobe washed the distance orange. Under the day cycle or a late r_time_of_day the open yard and the snow took the full moon like a pale blue day. A third of the moon and of the sky's fill, and an eye half as eager to open, leave a moonlit night that still reads.

2.$comment: Overcast valley. The original's grey cloud deck is its mood; the atmosphere alone drew a clear blue sky over it. At night the moon lit the valley mist into a pale blue glow over the whole sky. The mist is most of what a night here shows, so it takes far less than the first mission: the first's settings left the frame black. A dimmer moon and mist keep the silhouettes against a dark sky.

3.$comment: Night storm over the radar base. Thicker and flatter -- less forward scatter, more ambient -- under the original's slate storm sky. Its thick flat storm air lit by the moon stood over the base as a grey wall and turned the hills white; under a dimmer moon the hills go dark against the sky. The haze keeps three quarters of its light, so the storm mist still hangs over the base as a volume; at 0.4 it went dark and the fog was gone.

4.$comment: Hazy valley by day, which stays as it is. At night the valley sits under ridges the moon passes behind, and the moonlit sky, not the moon, was all that lit it then: the eye set itself by that bright sky and the ground went black, then the moon came out and lit the valley like a dim day. A quarter of the moon and eight times the night sky's own glow -- the light that owes nothing to the moon -- bring the two close, and a stop and a quarter of night keeps the moonlit frame a night. The fog keeps most of its glow, so the mist still hangs over the base.

5.$comment: The level's own FlatSky asks for very little; a blue high-altitude haze suits it. Its night takes the fourth mission's: a dimmer moon over a brighter night sky, so the moon passing behind a ridge is not the jump from a dim day to black.

6.$comment: Overcast airfield under the original's grey deck. Its night takes the fourth mission's: a dimmer moon over a brighter night sky, so the moon passing behind a ridge is not the jump from a dim day to black.

7.$comment: Snow at night under a navy sky. Sun almost overhead by day, so a forward lobe buys nothing; keep it soft and even. Its night takes the fourth mission's: a dimmer moon over a brighter night sky, so the moon passing behind a ridge is not the jump from a dim day to black.

$comment: This level's authored sun is 55 degrees BELOW the horizon.
Nothing is lit by it, so the fog leans on ambient instead of pretending otherwise.

9.$comment: Rail yard in a bowl at night, in rain. Dense and low, so it collects between the cuttings.

10.$comment: Overcast train yard in rain under the original's grey deck.

11.$comment: Alpine prison at night, played from high on the mountains over the base in the valley. The level's own fog is a dark navy, and at night the medium caught so little light that it only dimmed the valley: thicker air alone changed nothing anyone could see, and the base sat crisp at the foot of the slope. Dense air pooled low (a 30 m falloff, a tenth kept at every height) and lit two and a half times as strongly at night shows as a mist over the valley that veils the base and fades the far ridges.

13.$comment: The power station under the original's red dusk sky, which is the mission. The haze takes the level's own red (its GlobalLight fog, 0.19 0.12 0.13), or the far hills fog white against a red sky.

igi2:$comment: I.G.I. 2. Each entry was set against the same view on the original's own picture (gfx_preset vanilla), at the
mission's opening and its own hour, until the ground under the player read as bright as it does there.
The sequel's night levels author their sun AS the moon, so the modern presets' fourfold moon and open eye,
which lift the first game's faint cycle moon into a readable night, land on a light that was already the
night its artists meant: the first mission came up four and a half times as bright as the original's. An
eighth of the moon, a third of the sky's fill and the original's own adaptation put it back.
Its day levels author no night to scale, and most are a dusk, an overcast or a red evening that the eye's
adaptation opened into a plain bright day; exposureStops closes it again by as much as each one needed.

igi2:11.$comment: Night over the Carpathian oil depot. Read as a pale blue day: the moonlit ground and tanks stood white.

igi2:13.$comment: Snow slopes in a blue dusk, not a clear noon.

igi2:14.$comment: Dark overcast valley under a storm deck.

igi2:15.$comment: The same valley and the same deck, at the bridge.

igi2:21.$comment: Libyan harbour at dusk; close already.

igi2:22.$comment: The prison cell, which the dynamic lighting leaves darker than the original's bake does. More than this only burns out the lit doorway: the walls are short of light, not of exposure.

igi2:24.$comment: Clear desert day; the sky wants it down a little and the sand does not.

igi2:25.$comment: Desert seen from the truck; close already.

igi2:26.$comment: The docks at night under floodlights. The moonlit concrete read as snow by day.

igi2:33.$comment: The temple under a red evening.

igi2:34.$comment: Inside the temple, lit by its own lamps; a stop brighter to the original's.

igi2:36.$comment: The same dusk at the launch site.

$comment: Empty deliberately. Every centre here has to be flown to and read off -- a guessed one is not
a weak volume, it is a volume somewhere else entirely, and it does nothing at all. The shape
each entry takes, for when they are authored:
"1": [ { "shape": "box",    // or "sphere", which uses extent.x as its radius
"centre": [6000.0, -13600.0, 42590.0],   // absolute world metres, from -camlog
"extent": [18.0, 26.0, 7.0],             // half-extents
"densityScale": 3.5 } ]                  // below 1 thins, above 1 thickens
